title: The future: imperfective and perfective
objectives: I can form the two futures of an imperfective verb, the compound 'бу́ду чита́ти' and the synthetic 'чита́тиму', and the future of a perfective verb, 'прочита́ю'.
I can choose the imperfective future for a process, a repeated action or an activity, and the perfective future for one completed result.
I can say what will happen if or when something else happens, with the future after 'якщо́' and 'коли́' where English uses the present.
I can place plans in time with 'че́рез ти́ждень', 'пі́сля робо́ти' and 'насту́пного ро́ку', and say how sure I am with 'обов’язко́во' and 'напе́вно'.
I can plan a trip, with tickets, a hotel and the days to leave and come back, and promise to meet someone at the station.
I can explain why 'обов’язко́во' has an apostrophe, why 'по́дорож' ends in a voiced [ʒ] and why 'квито́к' becomes 'квитка́'.

vocabulary.note: The present is 'плану́ю', 'плану́єш', 'плану́ють': '-ува-' becomes '-у-', as in 'працюва́ти', 'працю́ю'. The perfective partner is 'запланува́ти', made with the prefix 'за-'. The thing planned is an accusative object, or an infinitive follows: 'Я плану́ю подорожува́ти.'

example.source: What are you planning for the weekend?

vocabulary.note: It is made from the noun 'по́дорож', trip, with the suffix '-ува-', and its present is 'подорожу́ю', 'подорожу́єш', 'подорожу́ють'. It means to make trips, usually for pleasure. It has no perfective partner in everyday use, so its future is always 'бу́ду подорожува́ти' or 'подорожува́тиму'.

example.source: In the summer we will travel.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'по́дорожі'. It is feminine although it ends in a consonant, as 'сіль' and 'о́сінь' are, so its adjectives are feminine: 'ціка́ва по́дорож'. Its accusative is the same as its nominative, as for every feminine noun in a consonant.

example.source: It will be an interesting trip.

vocabulary.note: It names the breaks in the school or university year, above all the long summer break. Like 'штани́', it has only plural forms, so the verb and the adjectives with it are plural: 'бу́дуть кані́кули'. A working adult has 'відпу́стка' instead.

example.source: We will have our break soon.

vocabulary.note: It names the time off that an employee takes from work. To be on vacation is 'бу́ти у відпу́стці', where 'к' becomes 'ц' before the locative ending '-і', as 'апте́ка' becomes 'в апте́ці'. The word comes from a verb meaning to let someone go.

example.source: Mom is on vacation now.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'мо́ря'. A stay by the sea takes 'на', as open places do: 'на мо́рі', at the sea, with the locative, and 'на мо́ре', to the sea, with the accusative. 'Бі́ля мо́ря' is near the sea.

example.source: Oksana wants to go to the sea.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'квитка́', plural 'квитки́'. The 'о' of the last syllable appears only in the nominative and accusative singular and drops in all the other forms, as 'ри́нок' becomes 'ри́нку'. A ticket to an event is 'квито́к на' with the accusative ('квито́к на конце́рт'), and a ticket to a city is 'квито́к до' with the genitive ('квито́к до Льво́ва').

example.source: I will buy two tickets.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'готе́лю', locative 'у готе́лі'. A building takes '-у' in the genitive, as 'магази́ну' does, and after a soft stem that ending is written '-ю'. The 'ль' at the end is soft.

example.source: Our hotel will be near the sea.

vocabulary.note: It is made from 'обо́в’язок', duty, and literally means 'obligatorily', as a duty requires. In speech it turns a plan into a firm promise, and said alone it is a strong 'yes, definitely'. In 'обо́в’язок' the stress falls on the second 'о'; in the adverb it falls on the last syllable but one.

example.source: I will definitely read this book.

vocabulary.note: It says that the speaker thinks something is likely. At the start of a sentence it is set off by a comma. 'Напе́вно, ні.' means 'Probably not.' The 'в' before 'н' is [w].

example.source: It will probably rain tomorrow.

vocabulary.note: It says that something will happen a short time from now. It usually stands before the verb.

example.source: Oksana will be back soon.

vocabulary.note: With a word of time in the genitive and no preposition, it says when: 'насту́пного ро́ку', next year; 'насту́пного ти́жня', next week; 'насту́пної субо́ти', next Saturday. This is the genitive of time from the unit on the past, as in 'мину́лого ти́жня'.

example.target: Насту́пного ти́жня я бу́ду у Льво́ві.
example.source: Next week I will be in Lviv.
example.source_literal: Of-next of-week I will-be in Lviv.

vocabulary.note: It has a soft stem, like 'си́ній': 'майбу́тня', 'майбу́тнє', 'майбу́тні'. The future tense is 'майбу́тній час', as the present tense is 'тепе́рішній час'.

example.source: Today we are studying the future tense.

vocabulary.note: It takes the genitive and names the event or period after which something happens: 'пі́сля робо́ти', 'пі́сля конце́рту', 'пі́сля відпу́стки'.

example.source: After the concert we will go for a walk.

vocabulary.source: in, after a period; through, across
vocabulary.note: It takes the accusative. With a length of time it counts the time from now until something happens: 'че́рез ти́ждень', in a week, a week from now. With a place it means through or across: 'че́рез парк'. The final 'з' stays voiced: [z].

example.source: I will be back in an hour.

vocabulary.note: It introduces a real condition, one that may or may not be met. When the condition lies in the future, the verb after 'якщо́' is in the future, where English uses the present.

example.target: Якщо́ ти хо́чеш, ми бу́демо подорожува́ти ра́зом.
example.source: If you want, we will travel together.

vocabulary.note: The perfective partner is 'пообіця́ти'. The 'ц' is soft before 'я'. 'Обіця́ю!' alone means 'I promise!', and what is promised follows 'що' ('Я обіця́ю, що бу́ду там.'). The person promised to is in the dative, the case of the next unit.

example.source: Do you promise that you will meet me?

vocabulary.note: The perfective partner is 'поверну́тися': 'поверну́ся', 'пове́рнешся', 'пове́рнуться', with the stress moving back to the stem after the 'я' form. Here '-ся' is part of the verb and adds no meaning of its own; without it, 'поверта́ти' is to turn, from the unit on directions.

example.source: When will you come back from the sea?

vocabulary.note: The perfective partner is 'почека́ти', to wait for a while. The person or thing waited for stands straight after the verb ('Я чека́ю тебе́.') or after 'на' with the accusative ('Я чека́ю на те́бе.'); both mean 'I am waiting for you'.

example.source: Oksana waited a long time for the bus.

vocabulary.note: The future is 'зустрі́ну', 'зустрі́неш', 'зустрі́нуть', on a stem with an 'н' that the infinitive does not show. The imperfective partner is 'зустріча́ти'. The person met is in the accusative, and the verb also means to meet someone who arrives, at a station for example. To meet up with friends by arrangement is 'зустріча́тися', from the unit on the past.

example.source: I will meet you at the station.

dialogues.title: A trip to the sea
dialogues.context: At the end of the spring term, Oksana and Sam talk about the summer in a café. They are friends and say 'ти'. Odesa, 'Оде́са', is a city on the Black Sea.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Се́ме, що ти бу́деш роби́ти влі́тку?
lines.source: Sam, what are you going to do this summer?
lines.source_literal: Sam, what you will-be to-do in-summer?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ще не зна́ю. Напе́вно, бу́ду працюва́ти. А ти?
lines.source: I don't know yet. I'll probably work. And you?
lines.source_literal: Still not I-know. Probably, I-will-be to-work. And you?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Незаба́ром у ме́не бу́дуть кані́кули, і я ду́же хо́чу на мо́ре.
lines.source: My break starts soon, and I really want to go to the sea.
lines.source_literal: Soon at me will-be break, and I very want on sea.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: На мо́ре? Я теж! Ми мо́жемо подорожува́ти ра́зом.
lines.source: To the sea? Me too! We can travel together.
lines.source_literal: On sea? I too! We can to-travel together.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: До́бре! Коли́ в те́бе бу́де відпу́стка?
lines.source: Great! When will you have your vacation?
lines.source_literal: Good! When at you will-be vacation?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Че́рез ти́ждень. У п’я́тницю я закі́нчу вели́ку робо́ту.
lines.source: In a week. On Friday I'll finish a big job.
lines.source_literal: Through week. In Friday I will-finish big work.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Я сього́дні куплю́ квитки́ на субо́ту.
lines.source: I'll buy tickets for Saturday today.
lines.source_literal: I today will-buy tickets on Saturday.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́бре. А готе́ль? Він бу́де дороги́й?
lines.source: Good. And the hotel? Will it be expensive?
lines.source_literal: Good. And hotel? It will-be expensive?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Напе́вно, ні. Я зна́ю мали́й готе́ль бі́ля мо́ря.
lines.source: Probably not. I know a small hotel near the sea.
lines.source_literal: Probably, no. I know small hotel near sea.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А до́вго ми там бу́демо?
lines.source: And will we be there long?
lines.source_literal: And long we there will-be?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ти́ждень. Ми бу́демо гуля́ти, ї́сти ри́бу й відпочива́ти.
lines.source: A week. We'll go for walks, eat fish and relax.
lines.source_literal: Week. We will-be to-stroll, to-eat fish and to-rest.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А якщо́ бу́де дощ?
lines.source: And what if it rains?
lines.source_literal: And if will-be rain?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Якщо́ бу́де дощ, ми бу́демо сиді́ти в кафе́ й пи́ти ка́ву.
lines.source: If it rains, we'll sit in a café and drink coffee.
lines.source_literal: If will-be rain, we will-be to-sit in café and to-drink coffee.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ду́же до́бре! Я обов’язко́во ї́ду.
lines.source: Very good! I'm definitely going.
lines.source_literal: Very well! I obligatorily go.

dialogues.title: I'll meet you at the station
dialogues.context: Olena is on vacation at the sea and phones her brother Taras. She is coming back to Kyiv by train on Sunday. Brother and sister say 'ти'.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Тара́се, приві́т! Я поверта́юся в неді́лю.
lines.source: Hi, Taras! I'm coming back on Sunday.
lines.source_literal: Taras, hi! I return in Sunday.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Приві́т! У неді́лю? О котрі́й?
lines.source: Hi! On Sunday? At what time?
lines.source_literal: Hi! In Sunday? At which?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: О сьо́мій ве́чора, на вокза́лі. Ти мене́ зустрі́неш?
lines.source: At seven in the evening, at the station. Will you meet me?
lines.source_literal: At seventh of-evening, on station. You me will-meet?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Звича́йно, зустрі́ну.
lines.source: Of course I will.
lines.source_literal: Of-course, I-will-meet.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Мину́лого лі́та ти теж обіця́в, а я чека́ла годи́ну.
lines.source: Last summer you promised too, and I waited an hour.
lines.source_literal: Of-last of-summer you too promised, and I waited hour.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ви́бач! Але́ в неді́лю я обов’язко́во бу́ду там.
lines.source: Sorry! But on Sunday I'll definitely be there.
lines.source_literal: Sorry! But in Sunday I obligatorily will-be there.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: А ти не бу́деш працюва́ти?
lines.source: Won't you be working?
lines.source_literal: And you not will-be to-work?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ні. Я закі́нчу робо́ту о шо́стій і бу́ду на вокза́лі о пів на сьо́му.
lines.source: No. I'll finish work at six and be at the station at half past six.
lines.source_literal: No. I will-finish work at sixth and will-be on station at half on seventh.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: А якщо́ ти не закі́нчиш о шо́стій?
lines.source: And what if you don't finish at six?
lines.source_literal: And if you not will-finish at sixth?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Закі́нчу, обіця́ю! Я чека́тиму на пло́щі бі́ля вокза́лу.
lines.source: I will, I promise! I'll wait on the square by the station.
lines.source_literal: I-will-finish, I-promise! I will-wait on square near station.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Дя́кую! А я куплю́ для те́бе смачну́ ри́бу.
lines.source: Thanks! And I'll buy you some tasty fish.
lines.source_literal: I-thank! And I will-buy for you tasty fish.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ри́бу? Я бу́ду там о шо́стій!
lines.source: Fish? I'll be there at six!
lines.source_literal: Fish? I will-be there at sixth!

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: До неді́лі, Тара́се!
lines.source: See you on Sunday, Taras!
lines.source_literal: Until Sunday, Taras!

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Бува́й, Оле́но!
lines.source: Bye, Olena!

dialogues.title: Plans for next year
dialogues.context: At the last lesson before the summer break, Iryna Petrivna asks Sam about his plans. Teacher and student say 'ви' to each other. Iryna Petrivna often uses the one-word future, such as 'роби́тимете'.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Се́ме, що ви плану́єте на насту́пний рік?
lines.source: Sam, what are you planning for next year?
lines.source_literal: Sam, what you plan for next year?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Насту́пного ро́ку я бу́ду вивча́ти украї́нську мо́ву тут, у Ки́єві.
lines.source: Next year I'll study Ukrainian here in Kyiv.
lines.source_literal: Of-next of-year I will-be to-study Ukrainian language here, in Kyiv.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Ду́же до́бре! А в Кана́ду ви не пове́рнетеся?
lines.source: Very good! And won't you go back to Canada?
lines.source_literal: Very well! And to Canada you not will-return?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Поверну́ся, але́ не за́раз. Напе́вно, насту́пної зими́.
lines.source: I will, but not now. Probably next winter.
lines.source_literal: I-will-return, but not now. Probably, of-next of-winter.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: А що ви роби́тимете влі́тку?
lines.source: And what will you do in the summer?
lines.source_literal: And what you will-do in-summer?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Улі́тку я відпочива́тиму на мо́рі, в Оде́сі. Окса́на теж ї́де.
lines.source: In the summer I'll be relaxing at the sea, in Odesa. Oksana is going too.
lines.source_literal: In-summer I will-rest on sea, in Odesa. Oksana too goes.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Яка́ га́рна по́дорож! А ви бу́дете чита́ти влі́тку?
lines.source: What a lovely trip! And will you read over the summer?
lines.source_literal: What-kind nice trip! And you will-be to-read in-summer?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Обов’язко́во! Обіця́ю, що бу́ду чита́ти щодня́.
lines.source: Definitely! I promise I'll read every day.
lines.source_literal: Obligatorily! I-promise, that I-will-be to-read every-day.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Поба́чимо! А коли́ ви пове́рнетеся, ми прочита́ємо нову́ кни́гу.
lines.source: We'll see! And when you come back, we'll read a new book.
lines.source_literal: We-will-see! And when you will-return, we will-read new book.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А ви, Іри́но Петрі́вно? Що ви плану́єте?
lines.source: And you, Iryna Petrivna? What are you planning?
lines.source_literal: And you, Iryna Petrivna? What you plan?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: У ме́не бу́де відпу́стка. Моя́ сестра́ живе́ у Льво́ві, і я бу́ду там ти́ждень.
lines.source: I'll have my vacation. My sister lives in Lviv, and I'll spend a week there.
lines.source_literal: At me will-be vacation. My sister lives in Lviv, and I will-be there week.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А пі́сля відпу́стки?
lines.source: And after your vacation?
lines.source_literal: And after vacation?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Пі́сля відпу́стки я чека́тиму на вас тут.
lines.source: After my vacation I'll be waiting for you here.
lines.source_literal: After vacation I will-wait on you here.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́бре! До поба́чення, Іри́но Петрі́вно!
lines.source: Good! Goodbye, Iryna Petrivna!
lines.source_literal: Good! Until seeing, Iryna Petrivna!

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: по́дорож, обов’язко́во, готе́ль and the other new words
grammar.explanation:
The new words of this unit can be read with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress. The points below are the ones that are easy to miss.

'По́дорож' [ˈpɔdɔrɔʒ] ends in 'ж', and it stays voiced, as every voiced consonant does at the end of a Ukrainian word: the word ends in the sound of the 's' in 'measure', never in the 'sh' of 'shoe'. The same rule keeps the final 'з' of 'че́рез' a [z]. 'По́дорож' is feminine although it ends in a consonant, as 'сіль' and 'о́сінь' are, and its genitive is 'по́дорожі'. The spelling does not show this gender, so it is learned with the word.

In 'обов’язко́во' [ɔbɔʋjɑzˈkɔʋɔ] the apostrophe stands after 'в' and before 'я'. As in 'м’я́со' and 'п’ять', it keeps the 'в' hard and makes the 'я' a full [jɑ] with its [j] sounded. The 'з' before 'к' stays voiced. Voicing changes in one direction only: a voiceless consonant before a voiced one becomes voiced, as in 'вокза́л', but a voiced consonant before a voiceless one keeps its voice, apart from the 'г' of 'ле́гко'. 'Відпу́стка' keeps its [d] before 'п' in the same way.

The letter 'в' shows both of its sounds in this unit: [ʋ] before a vowel ('обов’язко́во', 'поверта́тися') and [w], as in 'cow', before a consonant: 'напе́вно' [nɑˈpɛwnɔ].

In 'готе́ль' [ɦɔˈtɛlʲ] the 'т' is hard before 'е', and the soft sign makes the final 'л' soft. The 'л' stays soft in the other forms, where the vowel letter after it shows the softness: genitive 'готе́лю', locative 'у готе́лі'.

Two alternations taught with the locative and the genitive appear in the new words:

- 'квито́к' keeps the 'о' of its last syllable only in the nominative and accusative singular and loses it in every other form: 'квитка́', 'квитки́', as 'ри́нок' becomes 'ри́нку'.
- 'відпу́стка' has 'к' before most endings and 'ц' before the locative ending '-і': 'у відпу́стці', as 'апте́ка' gives 'в апте́ці'.

The reflexive verbs have the clusters of the unit on daily routine: in 'поверта́ється' the '-ться' is [t͡sʲːɑ], and in 'пове́рнешся' the '-шся' is [sʲːɑ].

Stress behaves in two different ways in the new verb forms. In the perfective 'поверну́тися' it moves: the 'я' form is stressed on the ending and the other forms on the stem ('поверну́ся', 'пове́рнешся', 'пове́рнеться'). In the synthetic future of the next note it never moves: it stays on the syllable stressed in the infinitive, however many syllables the ending adds ('чита́ти', 'чита́тимемо'; 'подорожува́ти', 'подорожува́тимуть').

rows: at the end of a word
at the end of a word
at the end of a word

examples.source: What an interesting trip!
I will definitely be there.
Our hotel is close by.
We will buy the tickets today.
He will be back in a week.

grammar.title: Three futures: бу́ду чита́ти, чита́тиму and прочита́ю
grammar.explanation:
English makes its future with a helping word, 'will'. Ukrainian has three ways to make the future, and which one a verb uses depends on its aspect, the choice between a process and a completed whole taught in the unit on aspect. An imperfective verb has two futures, which mean the same thing. A perfective verb has one.

The compound future is made of two words: the future of 'бу́ти' ('бу́ду', 'бу́деш', 'бу́де', 'бу́демо', 'бу́дете', 'бу́дуть') and the infinitive of an imperfective verb. It is the future of the unit on weather and plans: 'Я бу́ду чита́ти.', 'Ми бу́демо відпочива́ти.' Only 'бу́ти' changes for the person; the infinitive stays as it is.

The synthetic future is one word: the infinitive of an imperfective verb with an ending added to it. 'Synthetic' means built into a single word, and 'compound' means built from two. The endings are:

- '-му' for 'я': 'чита́тиму'
- '-меш' for 'ти': 'чита́тимеш'
- '-ме' for 'він', 'вона́', 'воно́': 'чита́тиме'
- '-мемо' for 'ми': 'чита́тимемо'
- '-мете' for 'ви': 'чита́тимете'
- '-муть' for 'вони́': 'чита́тимуть'

These endings are the same for every verb, whatever its conjugation. A reflexive verb puts '-ся' at the very end, after the new ending: 'поверта́тимуся', 'поверта́тимешся', 'поверта́тиметься'. The two imperfective futures are equally correct and mean the same, and speakers use both, often in one conversation: 'Що ви бу́дете роби́ти?' and 'Що ви роби́тимете?' both ask 'What will you do?'.

The perfective future has no special form. The unit on aspect showed that a perfective verb has no present, and that its forms with present endings are its future: 'прочита́ю', I will read; 'зроблю́', I will do; 'куплю́', I will buy; 'візьму́', I will take; 'дам', I will give. Neither 'бу́ду' nor the synthetic endings ever go with a perfective verb, because its own forms already mean 'will'.

'Бу́ти' itself uses the forms 'бу́ду', 'бу́деш' and so on alone for 'will be': 'За́втра я бу́ду вдо́ма.' In possession the thing owned is the subject, so the verb agrees with it, as 'був' and 'була́' do in the past: 'У ме́не бу́де відпу́стка.', 'У нас бу́дуть кані́кули.' What there will not be is in the genitive after 'не бу́де', as after 'не було́': 'За́втра не бу́де дощу́.'

As in English, the present can also name an arrangement already fixed for the near future: 'У субо́ту я працю́ю.', I am working on Saturday; 'За́втра ми ї́демо на мо́ре.', Tomorrow we are going to the sea.

examples.source: Tomorrow I will work.
We will go for a walk in the park.
What will you do tomorrow?
I will read this book.
We will have a break.
There will be no rain tomorrow.

grammar.title: Imperfective or perfective future
grammar.explanation:
The choice between the two aspects works in the future exactly as it does in the past. What decides is how the speaker presents the action, not how long it takes.

The imperfective future presents an action as a process, a repetition or an activity in general, with no attention to a result:

- a process that lasts: 'Я бу́ду працюва́ти до ве́чора.', I will be working until the evening.
- a repeated action: 'Улі́тку я бу́ду чита́ти щодня́.', In the summer I will read every day.
- an activity, as in the answer 'Бу́ду відпочива́ти.', I'll relax, to the question 'Що ти бу́деш роби́ти?', What will you be doing?

The perfective future presents one action as a completed whole with a result:

- one finished result: 'Я прочита́ю кни́гу за́втра.', I will read the book tomorrow, to the end.
- steps in a series, each finished before the next begins: 'Споча́тку я куплю́ квитки́, а по́тім зустрі́ну Окса́ну.', First I'll buy the tickets, and then I'll meet Oksana.
- a promise of a result: 'Я обов’язко́во це зроблю́.', I will definitely do it.

English often says both with the same 'will', so the English sentence does not decide the aspect. 'Я бу́ду писа́ти', I will be writing, says what the speaker will be busy with; 'Я напишу́', I will write it, says that the writing will be done. The questions 'Що ти бу́деш роби́ти?', What will you be doing?, and 'Що ти зро́биш?', What will you get done?, differ in the same way: the first asks about activities, the second about what will get done.

The words that point to the imperfective in the past do the same in the future: 'до́вго', 'ча́сто' and 'щодня́'. 'Обов’язко́во', 'напе́вно' and 'незаба́ром' go with either aspect.

The new verbs of this unit come in pairs like those of the unit on aspect, as the table shows. 'Подорожува́ти' has no perfective partner in everyday use, so its future is always imperfective. 'Поба́чити', the perfective of 'ба́чити', is common in the reply 'Поба́чимо!', We'll see!

grammar.title: The future after коли́ and якщо́, and words of time
grammar.explanation:
A clause is a part of a sentence with its own verb. In English, a clause with 'if' or 'when' about the future has its verb in the present: 'If it is warm, we will go for a walk.' Ukrainian puts both verbs in the future, because both actions are still to come:

- 'Якщо́ бу́де те́пло, ми бу́демо гуля́ти.', literally 'if will-be warm, we will-be to-stroll'.
- 'Коли́ я закі́нчу робо́ту, я бу́ду відпочива́ти.', literally 'when I will-finish work, I will-be to-rest'.

'Якщо́' introduces a condition that may or may not be met. 'Коли́', the question word 'when?' of the unit on weather and plans, also joins two clauses as 'when', for something expected to happen. Either clause can come first, and a comma always separates them: 'Ми бу́демо гуля́ти, якщо́ бу́де те́пло.' A condition that is only imagined, as in 'if I were rich', uses another word, taught with the conditional.

The aspect in a 'коли́' clause shows how the two actions fit together. A perfective says that one action will be finished before the other begins: 'Коли́ я закі́нчу робо́ту...', when I have finished work. An imperfective says that the two will happen at the same time: 'Коли́ я бу́ду в Оде́сі, я бу́ду гуля́ти бі́ля мо́ря.', When I am in Odesa, I will walk by the sea.

The word 'що', which is 'what' in a question, also joins a clause to a verb of saying, thinking or promising, as English 'that' does, and the clause has its own future: 'Я ду́маю, що за́втра бу́де те́пло.', I think it will be warm tomorrow; 'Я обіця́ю, що бу́ду там.', I promise that I will be there. Ukrainian always writes a comma before it.

Four patterns say when a planned action happens:

- 'че́рез' with the accusative counts a length of time from now: 'че́рез ти́ждень', in a week; 'че́рез годи́ну', in an hour; 'че́рез дві годи́ни', in two hours.
- 'пі́сля' with the genitive names the event after which it happens: 'пі́сля робо́ти', after work; 'пі́сля конце́рту', after the concert.
- 'насту́пний' with a word of time in the genitive and no preposition names the next one: 'насту́пного ро́ку', next year; 'насту́пного ти́жня', next week; 'насту́пної субо́ти', next Saturday.
- 'на' with the accusative names the time a plan is for: 'Що ти плану́єш на вихідні́?', What are you planning for the weekend?; 'квитки́ на субо́ту', tickets for Saturday.

A length of time in the accusative with no preposition says how long something lasts: 'Ми бу́демо там ти́ждень.', We will be there for a week.

culture.title: Time off at the sea and in the mountains
culture.text:
Ukrainian has two words for time off. 'Кані́кули' are the breaks of schools and universities: short breaks during the year and the long summer break, which for schoolchildren lasts about three months. 'Відпу́стка' is leave from work. By law an employee in Ukraine has at least twenty-four calendar days of paid leave a year, and many people take it in the summer, often in two parts.

For a summer holiday Ukrainians have long chosen between two kinds of place:

- the sea: the coast of the Black Sea, 'Чо́рне мо́ре', with Odesa as its best-known city
- the mountains: the Carpathians, 'Карпа́ти', in the west, for walking in summer and skiing in winter

Many families also spend part of the summer in a village, at the house of a grandmother or other relatives, with a garden to look after.

Long trips inside Ukraine are often made by train. Overnight trains link Kyiv with Lviv, Odesa and Kharkiv, and tickets for summer travel sell out early, so people buy them well in advance. A plan is often confirmed with 'обов’язко́во', definitely, and a polite answer to an invitation the speaker is not sure about is 'Напе́вно, так.', probably, yes.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian with the English
Match each word or phrase with its meaning

choices: We will stay in an apartment.
We will stay in a hotel.
We will stay by the sea.

exercises.prompt: Sam works and takes two weeks off in the summer. Which word names his time off?
exercises.explanation: 'Відпу́стка' is leave from work. 'Кані́кули' are the breaks of schools and universities, and 'по́дорож' is a trip.

exercises.prompt: How many futures does an imperfective verb such as 'чита́ти' have?
choices: Two: 'бу́ду чита́ти' and 'чита́тиму', which mean the same
Three: one for each person in the singular
exercises.explanation: An imperfective verb has a compound future and a synthetic future, with the same meaning. 'Прочита́ю' is the future of the perfective partner 'прочита́ти'.
The compound future is the future of 'бу́ти' plus an imperfective infinitive. For 'я' the form is 'бу́ду'.
Only 'бу́ти' changes for the person: 'бу́деш' for 'ти'. The infinitive 'відпочива́ти' stays as it is.

exercises.prompt: Which form is the synthetic future of 'працюва́ти' for 'ми'?
exercises.explanation: The synthetic future is the infinitive plus an ending, and the ending for 'ми' is '-мемо'. 'Працю́ємо' is the present, 'працюва́ли' the past and 'працюва́тимуть' the future for 'вони́'.

exercises.hint_source: They will go for a walk by the sea.
exercises.explanation: Both imperfective futures are correct: the synthetic 'гуля́тимуть', with the ending '-муть' for 'вони́', and the compound 'бу́дуть гуля́ти'.

exercises.prompt: Which is the synthetic future of 'поверта́тися' for 'я'?
exercises.explanation: The ending '-му' goes after the infinitive, and '-ся' moves to the very end. 'Поверта́юся' is the present, and 'поверну́ся' is the future of the perfective partner 'поверну́тися'.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'Я прочита́ю' mean 'I will read' although it has a present ending?
choices: The prefix 'про-' is a sign of the future in every verb
'Прочита́ти' is perfective, and a perfective verb has no present: its forms with present endings are its future
exercises.explanation: A perfective presents an action as a completed whole, which cannot be happening at the moment of speaking, so its present-looking forms refer to the future.

exercises.hint_source: Tomorrow I will read this book to the end.
exercises.explanation: One finished result takes the perfective future, the 'я' form of 'прочита́ти'.

exercises.hint_source: I will get it done today.
exercises.explanation: Getting something done is one action with a result, so the perfective 'зроби́ти' is used: 'зроблю́', with the 'л' inserted after 'б', as in 'роблю́'.

choices: Taras met Olena at the station.
Taras will wait for Olena at the station.
Taras will meet Olena at the station.

exercises.prompt: Taras asks Olena 'Що ти бу́деш роби́ти в неді́лю?' What is he asking about?
choices: What she will be doing on Sunday, her activities
What she will have finished by Sunday
exercises.explanation: The imperfective future asks about activities. 'Що ти зро́биш?', with the perfective, would ask what she will get done.

exercises.prompt: 'I will finish the work, and then I will rest.' Which form says 'I will finish'?
exercises.explanation: The first step of a series is finished before the next begins, so it takes the perfective future 'закі́нчу'. 'Бу́ду закі́нчувати' presents the finishing as a process, and 'закі́нчувала' is a past form.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'In the summer I will read every day'?
exercises.explanation: A repeated action takes the imperfective future, here the synthetic 'чита́тиму'. The first sentence means 'In the summer I will read the book', and the third is in the past.

exercises.prompt: In 'Якщо́ бу́де те́пло, ми бу́демо гуля́ти.', why is the verb after 'якщо́' in the future?
choices: Ukrainian puts a future condition in the future, where English uses the present
'Якщо́' is always followed by 'бу́де', whatever the time
Because 'те́пло' needs a verb of its own in every sentence
exercises.explanation: Both actions are still to come, so both verbs are in the future. English says 'If it is warm', with the present.

exercises.prompt_target: Якщо́ за́втра ___ дощ, ми бу́демо в кафе́.
exercises.hint_source: If it rains tomorrow, we will be in the café.
exercises.explanation: The condition lies in the future, so 'бу́ти' is in the future: 'бу́де'. English uses the present, 'rains'.

exercises.prompt_target: Коли́ Тара́с ___ робо́ту, він бу́де на вокза́лі.
exercises.hint_source: When Taras finishes work, he will be at the station.
exercises.explanation: The 'коли́' clause is in the future, and the perfective 'закі́нчить' shows that the work will be finished before he is at the station.

choices: in a week, a week from now
exercises.explanation: 'Че́рез' with the accusative counts a length of time from now until something happens.

exercises.prompt: Which word completes 'Ми пове́рнемося ___ дві годи́ни.', 'We will come back in two hours'?
exercises.explanation: A length of time counted from now takes 'че́рез' with the accusative. 'Пі́сля' names an event, as in 'пі́сля робо́ти', and takes the genitive.

exercises.hint_source: Next year we will be in Odesa.
exercises.explanation: 'Next year' is the genitive of time with no preposition: 'насту́пного ро́ку', like 'мину́лого ти́жня'.

exercises.hint_source: I will be back after work.
exercises.explanation: 'Пі́сля' takes the genitive, and the genitive of 'робо́та' is 'робо́ти'.

exercises.prompt: Why is there an apostrophe in 'обов’язко́во'?
choices: It shows that the stress falls on the next syllable
It shows that a letter has been left out
It keeps the 'в' hard and makes the 'я' a full [jɑ] with its [j] sounded
exercises.explanation: After 'б', 'п', 'в', 'м', 'ф' and 'р' before 'я', 'ю', 'є' or 'ї', the apostrophe keeps the consonant hard and the [j] sounded, as in 'м’я́со'.

choices: In [ʃ], as in 'shoe', because it is the last sound
In [ʒ], as in the 's' of 'measure', because a voiced consonant stays voiced at the end of a word
In [ʒ] followed by a short vowel
exercises.explanation: Ukrainian keeps voiced consonants voiced at the end of a word, as 'хліб' ends in [b] and 'че́рез' in [z].

exercises.prompt: Which of these nouns is feminine?
exercises.explanation: 'По́дорож' is feminine although it ends in a consonant, like 'сіль': 'ціка́ва по́дорож', genitive 'по́дорожі'. 'Готе́ль' and 'квито́к' are masculine, and 'мо́ре' is neuter.

exercises.prompt: In 'квитка́', the genitive of 'квито́к', what has happened to the stem?
choices: The 'о' of the last syllable has dropped, as in 'ри́нок', 'ри́нку'
An 'а' has taken the place of the 'о'
The stress has moved to show the plural
exercises.explanation: The 'о' of 'квито́к' appears only in the nominative and accusative singular. Every other form drops it: 'квитка́', 'квитки́'.

choices: [w], as in 'cow', because a consonant follows
exercises.explanation: Before a consonant 'в' is [w]: [nɑˈpɛwnɔ]. Before a vowel it is [ʋ], and it never turns into [f].
